question.text: Why does an American-style option typically command a higher premium than an otherwise identical European-style option?

answer.text: Because the American option provides the additional flexibility of early exercise at any time before expiry
Because American options are traded on larger exchanges with more liquidity
Because American options have lower margin requirements
Because American options always expire on the last business day of the month

explanation.text: The Logic: An American-style option grants the holder the right to exercise at any time on or before expiry, while a European-style option can be exercised only on the expiry date. The American style is therefore a superset of the European style — every exercise opportunity available to the European holder is also available to the American holder, plus the option of early exercise. Because of that additional optionality, the American-style premium is, all else equal, at least as high as the corresponding European-style premium. The Trap: Exchange size, liquidity, lower margin requirements, or month-end expiry are not the drivers of the relative premium. The differentiator is the exercise window. Note: The cited NISM-Series-VIII workbook pages (60-61, 75, 157-158) define American options as exercisable any time on or before expiry, European options as exercisable only on expiry, and state that Indian index/stock options are European style. However, the explicit comparison that American-style options command a higher premium due to early-exercise flexibility was not located in the pages checked. The framing above is standard options-theory rather than a direct workbook citation.
